transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hello, Doctor. Thank you for seeing me. Well, I... I came in today because, honestly, I just can’t seem to get anything in order anymore. It’s gotten so bad. If you were to walk into my house right now and look at my kitchen table, you'd think a tornado hit it. It is just covered, absolutely covered, with things I need to do but can't seem to manage. 

There are all my husband’s appointment papers—he has the cardiologist and the eye doctor, and I’m supposed to be keeping track of his schedule—and they’re all mixed up with these church flyers for a committee I'm on, and notes from the senior center about things we're supposed to sign up for, and just... piles of half-finished to-do lists. I write half a list on the back of an envelope, lose it, start another one on a grocery receipt... 

And the worst part is, I pull up a chair, and I just sit there looking at this mountain of paper, and I don't know which thing to do first. I just stare at it. I can't decide where to start, so I just sit there, and I sit there, and before I know it, the sun is going down and the whole entire day is gone and I haven't done a single thing. It's just so overwhelming, and I don't understand why I can't just pick up one piece of paper and deal with it like a normal person.
How long has this problem with organizing and managing tasks been going on? Has it always been this way, or did it start at a particular time?

Well, it's... it's a bit hard to explain, because I suppose I've always been a little scatterbrained, you know? Even back when I took a few classes at the community college years ago, I'd always have loose papers floating around. But this... this absolute paralysis, where it's taking over my whole life and ruining my days? That is newer. 

I can pinpoint it, actually. It's been about a year and three months. Yes, a year and three months exactly, because that was right around the time my husband's health started taking a turn. He had that first scare, and suddenly the doctors were saying he couldn't drive himself anymore, and he needed all these follow-ups—the cardiologist, the bloodwork, the specialists. And overnight, it felt like, I became his... his secretary, his nurse, his schedule coordinator. 

Before that, I just had to worry about my own little things, you know? Making sure I got to church on time, or remembering to pick up milk. But a year and three months ago, they handed me this massive folder of his medical instructions, and it was like a switch flipped in my brain. I brought that folder home, set it on the kitchen table, and it was like a black hole opened up. The papers just started multiplying. And ever since then, ever since he started needing me to manage his daily arrangements and appointments... I just can't do it. I sit there, looking at his appointment cards, and my brain just turns to mush. It's been fifteen months of just... staring at the table while the sun goes down.
Besides this difficulty organizing and managing tasks, how has your mood been over this past year and three months? Do you find yourself feeling sad, down, or hopeless?

Well, sad? I wouldn't say sad, exactly. Not hopeless, no. I mean, it's not like I'm sitting there crying at the kitchen table, you know? It's more just... frustration. Oh, the frustration is just immense. I sit there and I think, "Why can't you just do this, Helen? It's just a piece of paper. It's just a phone call to Dr. Miller's office to confirm the Tuesday appointment." But my brain just won't cooperate. 

So, no, I don't feel down in the dumps like a depressed person might. I still enjoy things when I can actually get to them. Like last week, my friend Martha came over—she's the one I'm on the church committee with, the flower guild, we do the arrangements for Sunday services—and we sat on the porch and had iced tea, and I felt perfectly fine. Happy, even! We were talking about the hydrangeas and how they're coming in this year, and I was laughing and feeling just like my old self. 

But then she left, and I had to go back inside and walk past that table... and that's when the heavy feeling hits. But it's not sadness. It's just this incredible weight of knowing I'm failing my husband when he needs me most. I feel guilty, maybe? And embarrassed. Oh, terribly embarrassed. If Martha had seen that table, I would have died of shame. I make sure to keep the door to the kitchen closed when anyone comes over now. But depressed? No, I don't think so. I just want my brain to work so I can get these things done. If I could just organize that table, I think I'd feel light as a feather.

Around the time your husband's health problems started—about 15 months ago—did you experience any significant health changes yourself? For example, did you have any head injuries, infections, high fevers, changes in medications you were taking, or any other medical events or diagnoses?

Oh, goodness, no. No, nothing like that at all. I've always been the healthy one, you see. That's part of why this whole situation is just so incredibly frustrating! I didn't fall and hit my head, I didn't have any terrible infections or high fevers... honestly, I rarely even get a sniffle when the grandkids come over with their winter colds. My immune system is like iron. 

And as for medications, I haven't changed a thing in years. I take a little calcium, you know, because at my age you have to think about your bones, and a standard multivitamin when I actually remember to buy them at the pharmacy, but no new prescriptions or anything like that. It was entirely my husband who had the health crisis. I was perfectly fine physically. I still am! I can walk down to the grocery store and back without losing my breath. 

So there was absolutely no physical reason for my brain to just... stop working the way it used to. I wasn't sick, I didn't have an accident, no new diagnoses for me, nothing. It was just the sudden avalanche of all his paperwork and his needs. I remember telling myself at the time, 'Well, Helen, at least you're healthy enough to take care of him,' but... well, what good is having a perfectly healthy body if I can't even manage to sort his cardiology bills from the church bulletin? It makes no sense to me, because physically, I haven't changed one bit.

When your husband's health crisis first happened 15 months ago, did you notice any changes in how you were feeling—like trouble sleeping, loss of appetite, or low energy—even before the paperwork piled up on the table? Or did everything feel completely normal until you actually sat down with all those medical documents?

Well... no, I didn't have any of those things. It's funny you ask that, because my sister, Margaret, she asked me the exact same thing when I first told her how I was struggling. She called me up—she lives in Florida now, moved down there right after her husband retired from the post office—and she said, "Helen, are you sleeping? Are you eating?" And I told her, "Margaret, I'm sleeping like a log." Because I was! And I still am. I put my head on the pillow at ten o'clock after I watch the evening news, and I am out until six in the morning. I've always been a good sleeper, thank the Lord. 

And my appetite? Oh, I wish I could say I lost my appetite! I really do. I could stand to lose a few pounds around the middle, to be perfectly honest with you. But no, I was eating just fine. I remember making a lovely pot roast that very first week after he came home from the hospital. I put in all the carrots and potatoes just the way he likes them, and we sat down and ate a hearty meal. And my energy was perfectly fine, too. Like I said, I was walking to the grocery store, I was keeping up with the house... physically, I was humming along just like a well-oiled machine. 

So, no, there wasn't any sort of... prelude, I guess you could say. There was no warning sign. I didn't feel run down or exhausted or anything like that. I felt completely, one hundred percent normal. It really was just the paperwork. It was the moment I sat down at that table with that big, blue folder they gave us at discharge. It had the hospital logo on the front—St. Jude's, a lovely hospital, the nurses were just angels—but I opened that folder, and I looked at the medication schedule, and the dietary restrictions, and the physical therapy referrals... and that was it. That was the exact moment my brain just... stopped. But before I opened it? I felt absolutely fine. Not a single thing wrong with me.

In those first few days or weeks after your husband came home from the hospital with that blue folder—before the table got piled up—did you notice any changes in how you felt emotionally? For instance, did you feel more anxious or worried about being able to handle everything, or did anything feel emotionally different to you at that time?

Well, anxious... I suppose anyone would be a little worried, wouldn't they? When you bring your husband home after something like that. But honestly, no, I wouldn't say I was pacing the floors or wringing my hands with worry. I mean, the doctors at St. Jude's were so thorough. Dr. Aris—such a wonderful young man, he had the nicest bedside manner, always took the time to explain things—he told me exactly what to expect. He said, "Helen, he's going to be tired, and he's going to need time." And I understood that. I really did. 

So when we first got home, I felt quite capable, actually. I remember walking him into the house, getting him settled in his favorite recliner—the brown leather one we bought when he retired, it has that nice lumbar support—and I felt like, "Okay, we can do this." I wasn't sitting there feeling terrified or overwhelmed by the idea of caring for him. I've always been a very capable person! When the kids were little, I managed the house, the PTA, the Sunday school... I was always juggling a dozen things. 

So no, I wasn't emotionally a wreck. I didn't feel this great sense of dread or anxiety about taking care of him. I was just focused on getting him comfortable. I made him some tea, I fluffed his pillows, and I felt quite calm about the whole situation. It wasn't an emotional problem at all. I wasn't sitting there crying or feeling like I couldn't handle it emotionally. It was just... the practical side of it. When I actually had to sit down and look at that blue folder and figure out the schedule and the bills and the insurance forms... that's when the trouble started. But emotionally? No, I felt fine. Just ready to do what needed to be done, you know?

You mentioned feeling guilty and embarrassed about the paperwork situation, and you said you'd feel 'light as a feather' if you could organize the table. But thinking back over these 15 months—has there been a general loss of interest or enjoyment in things you normally love, like your flower guild work at church or spending time with friends? Or do you still find pleasure in those activities when you're actually doing them?

Oh, heavens no. I still absolutely love the flower guild! In fact, that's one of the few things that keeps me sane these days. Just last Saturday, we were doing the arrangements for the Sunday morning service, and I brought in these gorgeous pink hydrangeas right out of my own backyard. I've been tending to those bushes for, oh, it must be twenty-five years now, ever since Pastor Miller was with us—he always loved the pink ones. Anyway, I was standing there in the church basement, snipping the stems and arranging them with some white lilies and a bit of baby's breath, and I just felt so happy. I really did. I haven't lost my joy for that at all.

And my friends! Oh, I still love seeing my friends. The girls and I meet for lunch at the Olive Garden every other Tuesday—we always ask for the corner booth so we can actually hear each other talk, you know how incredibly loud restaurants get these days, they just don't put any soundproofing in the ceilings anymore—but we sit there and we share the salad and breadsticks and we just laugh and laugh. I have a wonderful time with them. I don't sit there feeling sad or disconnected or anything like that. I'm right in the thick of the conversation, usually telling them all about what my grandchildren are up to. 

So no, I haven't lost interest in the things I love. I still love reading my historical fiction novels before bed, I still love baking my lemon pound cake for the church bake sales... I haven't stopped enjoying a single thing. I really do find just as much pleasure in them as I always have. It's really only when I'm home and I walk past that dining room table and see those stacks of medical bills and insurance statements that I feel that awful pit in my stomach. When I'm out doing my activities, or when I'm out in the garden with my pruning shears, I'm just as happy as a clam! I haven't lost my joy for life, doctor, not one bit. It's just... well, it's just that dratted paperwork that I can't seem to make my brain do. But my hobbies and my friends? Oh, I enjoy them just as much as ever.

You mentioned you still enjoy your flower guild work and your social activities. But when you're doing those things—arranging flowers, or planning what to bring to the church bake sale, or even managing your own personal tasks like gardening or cooking—do you find yourself able to make decisions and get started on things the way you normally would? Or do you experience that same kind of paralysis and difficulty deciding where to start in those areas too?

Well... see, that's the thing. That's exactly why I finally decided I needed to come in and see you. Because it's not just the medical folder anymore. I wish it was! But I just... I can’t seem to get anything in order anymore, no matter what it is. It's all bleeding together. 

If you were to walk into my house right now and look at my kitchen table... oh, it's just a crying shame. It used to be so pristine. I always kept a lovely lace runner on it that my grandmother tatted, with a nice bowl of fresh fruit right in the center. But now? It is absolutely covered. Just buried under everything. It's got my husband’s appointment papers and his physical therapy schedules, yes, but mixed right in with all of that are the church flyers for the upcoming Spring Jubilee that I'm supposed to be helping organize, and the senior-center notes—Mildred dropped off their new monthly newsletter because they changed the times for the water aerobics and the Tuesday matinees, and I told her I would look it over to see what we could attend. 

And on top of all of that, there are just... half-finished lists everywhere. I try to make a list, you know? I sit down with my good pen, the one with the blue ink that writes so smoothly, and a yellow legal pad, and I think, "Okay, Helen, let's figure out what you need to bake for the sale and what groceries we need." And I'll write down "flour" and "lemons"... and then my eye catches the church flyer, and I remember I need to call the guild about the vases, and then I see a doctor's bill peeking out from under the senior center schedule, and I just... I freeze. 

I sit there staring at this absolute mountain of paper, trying to figure out which single thing I am supposed to do first. Should I do the medical bills? Should I plan the baking? Should I read the newsletter? And my mind just goes completely blank. I literally sit there at that table, looking from one pile to the next, picking things up and putting them back down in the exact same spot, not knowing which thing to do first... and I do that until the whole day is gone. I'll look up at the clock on the microwave, and it's four-thirty in the afternoon, the sun is going down, my husband is asking what's for dinner, and I haven't accomplished a single solitary thing. Once I'm actually at the church with the flowers in my hand, I'm fine, but trying to organize it all at that table? I just can't do it anymore.

When you're at the church arranging flowers with the guild, or planning your bake sale items, do you ever find yourself stuck in that same way—unable to decide where to start or which task to do first—or does your mind work clearly and you're able to make decisions easily in those situations?

Well... no, no, not at all. That’s the most baffling part to me, to be completely honest with you. Because once I am physically there, doing the thing, my mind is just as clear as a bell. 

Take the flower guild, for instance. Once I'm actually standing down there in the church basement—it’s always a little chilly down there, you know, right next to the fellowship hall where they keep all the extra metal folding chairs—once I have my floral shears in my hand and my apron on, I don't freeze up for a single second. I can look at a whole bucket of gladiolus and some ferns and maybe some baby's breath, and I just *know* exactly which stem needs to be cut first. I know exactly how to angle it into the green floral foam so it looks full and balanced. I don't stand there agonizing over whether to put the pink one in first or the white one. It’s like second nature to me, my hands just know what to do and I don't feel confused at all.

And it’s the exact same way with the baking! If I'm standing at my kitchen counter, with my back turned to that dreadful dining room table, and I have my big yellow Pyrex mixing bowl out—the one my mother gave me for a wedding present back in 1974, it’s the largest one in the nested set and just absolutely perfect for a double batch of lemon pound cake—I don't get stuck. I know I need to cream the butter and the sugar first, and I know exactly when to add the eggs one by one. I don't stand there staring at the carton of eggs and the bag of flour wondering which one to touch first. I just get right to it, quick as a wink. 

It’s really only when I have to sit down and *plan* it out on paper, or when I'm looking at all those different pieces of information at once on the table, that my brain just completely stops working. But the actual doing of my hobbies? The physical act of arranging the flowers or mixing the batter? Oh, I can make those decisions without even blinking. It’s so incredibly frustrating, doctor, because I know I’m a capable woman, and I know my mind works perfectly fine when I'm holding a whisk or a pair of pruning shears... but put a stack of papers and lists in front of me and I might as well be on the moon!

When you're faced with just one simple task—like, let's say, just making a phone call to confirm your husband's appointment, or just writing out a grocery list by itself without looking at all the other papers—can you do that without getting stuck, or do you find yourself unable to get started even with that single thing?

Well, you see... that's the thing. If I could just sit down and do the one simple thing, maybe it wouldn't be so bad. But it never seems to be just the one thing, does it? Even if I tell myself, "Helen, just make this one phone call," by the time I find the number, I've already gotten distracted by something else, or I put it off because I think I need to find the insurance card first, and then... well, then I just completely forget. 

It's happening all the time lately. I’ll mean to do just one simple task, and it completely slips my mind. I’ve missed returning calls to my friends—and you know how much I love talking to them! I've left bills sitting right there under a stack of mail, completely forgetting they were even there until they're past due. My daughter, Sarah—she lives just two towns over, you know, over in Springfield, and she's always so busy with the kids' soccer practices and piano lessons—she’ll ask me to run a simple errand for her, like picking up some dry cleaning or dropping off a package at the post office, and I’ll promise her I will, and then... poof. Right out of my head. 

And the worst part, the part that really makes me feel just awful, is that more than once I’ve realized entirely too late that I never confirmed one of my husband’s appointments. Just the other week, Dr. Evans’ office called—he’s the cardiologist, a lovely man, always wears those colorful bow ties—they called on a Tuesday to confirm a Thursday appointment, and I wrote it down on a little pink sticky note. I stuck it right on the edge of the telephone base. But then I needed to wipe down the counter, so I moved the sticky note to the pile of mail, and... well, Thursday morning rolled around, and my husband was sitting in his armchair reading the paper, and I suddenly realized we were supposed to be at the clinic in twenty minutes! We rushed out the door in an absolute panic. So, no, even the simple things... I just can't seem to hold onto them in my head long enough to actually get them done.

Have you noticed any changes in your memory itself—like forgetting words, or losing track of conversations, or feeling confused about things that used to be clear to you? Or is it more that you can remember things fine, but you just can't seem to make yourself organize or act on them?

Oh, goodness no, it’s definitely not my memory itself! I know people my age start worrying about those sorts of things, but I assure you, my memory is as sharp as a tack. I never forget a word I’m trying to say, and I can follow a conversation just fine—even when my daughter Sarah is talking a mile a minute about all her kids' different soccer schedules and piano recitals. I remember exactly what I’m supposed to be doing. That's what makes it so agonizing! The problem isn't forgetting... it’s that when it comes time to actually do the mental work, I just... I can't. 

Like, when there’s a form to fill out, or those dreadful insurance papers to read, or even if I just need to sit down and put a program schedule together for the church... I keep finding little reasons to put it off. I really do. Because my head feels completely worn out before I even start! Just looking at the paperwork makes me feel exhausted. 

Take last week, for example. We got this new packet from the supplemental Medicare people—thick as a phone directory, printed on that terribly thin paper that tears if you look at it wrong—and I knew I needed to review the changes to my husband's physical therapy coverage. I sat down at that messy table, I looked at the envelope, and I suddenly thought, "You know, I really ought to water the African violets first, they're looking a little droopy." So I got up and did that. Then I came back, looked at the form again, and thought, "Well, I simply cannot focus on this without a proper cup of Earl Grey tea." So off I went to the kitchen to put the kettle on, and while I was waiting for it to boil, I decided I needed to wipe down the cabinet doors. 

I just kept finding all these little excuses, one after another, because the mere thought of reading through all that dense jargon or filling out the forms... it makes my brain feel heavy. It’s like I’ve run a marathon and I haven't even picked up my pen yet! And it's the exact same with the church activities. I remember every single detail—I know Mildred is bringing her pecan pie to the bake sale, and I know Susan is doing her famous brownies, my memory of who volunteered is crystal clear! But trying to force myself to sit down and actually organize it into a program schedule? I’ll go scrub the baseboards instead. I just feel so mentally drained before I even begin, so I just avoid it entirely.

When you read something like a newspaper article or a book chapter—something that requires you to focus and understand complex information—do you find that your mind can follow it clearly, or do you feel that same mental heaviness and difficulty concentrating that you described with the medical forms?

Oh, no, no, not at all. That’s another thing that just completely baffles me about this whole situation! When it comes to reading a book or the newspaper, I don't have that heavy feeling in the slightest. 

Every morning—well, except Sundays because we get the larger edition and my husband Arthur likes to read the front section first, he always has to check the local politics before he even touches his toast—but every weekday morning, I sit down with my coffee and I read the paper. I read all the long articles, the opinion pieces, even those complex investigative reports that go on for columns and columns, and I follow them perfectly fine. I don't lose my place or forget what the beginning of the article was about. 

And books! Goodness, doctor, I am quite the reader. I belong to a book club with some of the ladies from the neighborhood. We meet on the second Tuesday of every month, usually at Barbara's house because she has that lovely sunroom with the wicker furniture, and we read some very dense material. Just last month we read this terribly thick historical biography about Eleanor Roosevelt. It was fascinating, really, so many intricate details about her early life and her work with the UN, and I sat in my armchair and read it for hours at a time without any trouble at all. I didn't feel exhausted, my mind didn't wander off, and I certainly didn't suddenly feel the urge to go polish the silver instead of finishing the chapter. 

So it's really not the reading itself, or understanding complicated things, if that makes sense? If it's a story or an article, my brain just drinks it right in. It’s only when I have to *do* something with the information—like those dreadful Medicare forms where you have to cross-reference Part A with Part B, or making a schedule, or filling in little boxes—that's when that awful, heavy exhaustion sets in. But just reading a chapter in a book or the morning paper? Oh, I could do that all day long without my brain feeling tired in the least!

You mentioned that your memory is sharp and you can follow conversations just fine. But have you noticed any difficulty finding the right word when you're speaking, or any trouble understanding what people are saying to you? Has anyone commented that you're speaking differently than you used to?

Well, let me think... no. Heavens no, nothing like that at all. I’ve always had the gift of gab, you see, and that certainly hasn't changed one bit! You can ask my husband Arthur—he always jokes that I could talk the ear off a brass monkey. Even in the mornings, before he's really even finished his first cup of coffee, I’m already chatting away about whatever I’m reading in the paper or what needs doing around the house, and the words are always right there exactly when I need them. I never have to sit there snapping my fingers trying to remember what a certain thing is called or feeling like a word is stuck on the tip of my tongue. 

And as for understanding people... oh, I understand everyone perfectly fine. Like I mentioned with my daughter, Sarah, she talks an absolute mile a minute. I swear, that girl doesn't even stop to take a proper breath when she's telling me about little Timmy’s soccer coach or Emma’s piano instructor, but I follow every single word she says without a hitch. I never feel confused or like I'm missing the thread of the conversation, even when it's noisy or she's calling me from the car on her way to the grocery store. I know exactly what she's telling me. 

Nobody has said a word about me speaking differently, either. In fact, just at our last book club meeting at Barbara’s house, I was the one who led the discussion on the middle chapters of that Eleanor Roosevelt biography, and I had absolutely no trouble articulating my thoughts. I spoke for quite a while, actually! Barbara even told me I made some very insightful points about the political climate back then, and I didn't stumble over my words once. 

So, no, my vocabulary is just as good as it ever was, and I hear and understand folks clear as a bell. It’s just... well, like I was saying before, it's not the talking or the understanding that's the problem, it's the doing afterward. If Sarah asks me to pick up the dry cleaning while she's talking so fast, I understand her perfectly in the moment and I'll say all the right words back to agree to it, but then the follow-through just vanishes. But the words themselves? No, no trouble there at all.

Over these past 15 months, have you noticed any difficulty with things like balancing your checkbook, understanding your insurance paperwork when you actually sit down to read it carefully, or following the steps in a new recipe—tasks that require you to hold multiple pieces of information in mind at the same time and work through them in order?

Well, let me think about that. You're asking about understanding things like the checkbook or recipes, right? When I actually sit down and look at them? No, I don't have any trouble understanding them at all. None whatsoever. 

Take the checkbook, for instance. Arthur and I have had the same joint account at First National for forty-two years—since right after we bought this house, actually, because the previous bank was all the way across town and it was just too much of a hassle to drive over there every Friday to deposit his paycheck. I've always been the one to balance the ledger. And when I do sit down with it, I understand the math perfectly. I know exactly what needs to be subtracted, what checks haven't cleared yet, all of it. The numbers make perfect sense to me. The problem isn't understanding the math, it's just that I put off actually opening the book to do it! I'll look at the bank statement sitting on the counter and think, "Oh, I should really reconcile that," but then I'll notice the grout on the kitchen counter needs scrubbing, and before I know it, it's been three weeks and I haven't balanced it. But when I finally force myself to do it, the actual understanding of the numbers is fine.

And it's the exact same thing with recipes. Oh, I love to cook, doctor. I have this wonderful collection of recipes, some passed down from my mother, some I've clipped from magazines over the years. I have this one recipe for a very complicated beef Wellington—it has all these steps for the mushroom duxelles and wrapping the pastry just so. I read through the recipe and I understand every single step perfectly. I know exactly what it's asking me to do, in what order. I can picture the whole process in my head. There's no confusion at all. 

Even with that dreadful Medicare paperwork I was telling you about earlier. When I finally—and I mean finally, after I've watered the plants and made the tea and found every excuse under the sun—when I finally sit down and force my eyes to read the fine print, I understand what it says. I know what a deductible is, I understand the co-pays, I can follow the logic of it. It's just that the whole process of making myself sit there and work through it feels so overwhelmingly exhausting that I avoid it like the plague. 

So, no, I don't have any trouble understanding the steps or holding the information in my head once I'm actually doing it. My mind is perfectly clear on the *how* and the *what*. It's just the *doing* that's the hurdle! It's so frustrating to explain, because people think if you don't do something, it must be because you don't know how or you're confused. But I'm not confused in the slightest! I just... I just can't seem to make myself start these things, even though I understand them perfectly well.

Looking back over these past 15 months, do you feel like your thinking has become slower or less sharp than it used to be? For instance, do you find it takes you longer to understand things, or do you feel like your mind isn't as quick as it once was?

Oh, goodness no. No, not at all. If anything, I think I am just as sharp as a tack! You can ask Arthur about that, too. Every evening at seven o'clock—well, seven-thirty on Thursdays because the local news broadcast runs a bit long on the community calendar days—we sit down in the den with our chamomile tea and we watch Jeopardy. And I tell you, doctor, I am shouting out the answers before the contestants even have a chance to press their little buzzers! Just last night there was a whole category on nineteenth-century European monarchs, and I got every single one right, even the final question about Queen Victoria's uncle. Arthur always shakes his head and tells me he has no idea how I pull these facts out of thin air so quickly. 

So my mind is certainly not slowing down. It does not take me any longer to understand things than it did when I was thirty. When I am reading or watching a documentary, or even when I am just chatting with the neighbors over the fence, I catch on immediately. You know, Mildred next door is always going on about the neighborhood association rules, and they change those bylaws practically every month, but I can see exactly what the board is trying to do with the new landscaping restrictions before she even finishes explaining it to me. I never feel like I am lagging behind or struggling to process what is happening. 

It is really quite funny, in a terribly frustrating sort of way. My brain is going a mile a minute, sharp as ever, taking everything in perfectly. It is never a matter of me sitting there, staring blankly, trying to process what is going on. I process it instantly! I just cannot seem to channel that sharpness into actually doing the mundane tasks I need to do. But as far as my thinking slowing down or my mind losing its edge? No, absolutely not. I am just as quick on the draw as I have always been.

You've told me you're still sharp as a tack with things like Jeopardy and reading—but thinking back to 15 months ago before your husband's health crisis, do you feel like your mind is working at exactly the same speed and sharpness as it was back then, or have you noticed any gradual slowing down or decline in how quickly you can think through things compared to how you used to be?

Oh, compared to before Arthur's health crisis? Well... let me really think about that for a second. You know, fifteen months ago, before all the chaos with his heart started, we had such a lovely routine. We'd go to the farmer's market on Saturday mornings, and I'd have my whole list planned out in my head—first the tomatoes from the Johnson farm stand, then the fresh eggs from that nice young couple with the blue tent, and finally the sourdough bread from the bakery stall. And I suppose... well, I suppose you're asking if my mind was quicker back then.
